Architecture

How a SATOM node is put together — reverse proxy, gunicorn, the Flask application, PostgreSQL, the metrics store and the background services — and how two nodes form a primary/standby pair.

👤 ForAdministratorAdvanced user
📍 WhereServer side — /opt/satom on each node; the High Availability page is at /high-availability

Overview#

SATOM is a server-side web application. Browsers never talk to a Fortinet appliance directly: every request goes to the SATOM node, which reads its local database and, when an action needs it, calls the appliance's REST API (or SSH, for a few operations) on the user's behalf.

A node consists of one web application and a handful of small background services that share the same code base in /opt/satom and the same PostgreSQL database.

Component What it is Listens on Article
Reverse proxy nginx, terminates TLS and forwards to gunicorn :443 (and :80 → redirect) Installation
Web application gunicorn running the Flask app (wsgi:app) 127.0.0.1:8000 this article
Database PostgreSQL — configuration, users, audit, device cache local :5432 Data and storage
Rate-limit / cache store Redis, when RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI points at it local Configuration files
Metrics store VictoriaMetrics single node (satom-metrics.service) 127.0.0.1:8428 Data and storage
Scheduler python -m app.scheduler_runtime behind a primary-only guard — Services and timers
Reconciler python -m app.reconciler_runtime, keeps the pair's code in step — Services and timers
Privileged runner satom-updater.path + .service (root, on demand) — Security model
Timers alerts, certificate renewal, Sentinel responder, HA data sync — Services and timers

Request path#

  1. 1BrowserHTTPS to satom.example.com
  2. 2nginxTLS termination, HSTS, proxy_pass to 127.0.0.1:8000 with Host $http_host and X-Forwarded-*
  3. 3gunicorn4 worker processes, 600 s timeout (satom.service)
  4. 4Flask before_request gatesproduct (ADOM) gate → access gate (IP allow-list) → device gate → CSP nonce
  5. 5View (app/views)thin handler: parameters → service call → template or JSON
  6. 6Service (app/services)business logic; resolves REST paths through the endpoint registry
  7. 7Client / databaseREST call to the appliance, or a read from the local PostgreSQL cache
  8. 8after_requestsecurity headers, CSP, no-store on HTML

Reverse proxy#

The installer writes the nginx vhost itself (via deploy/tls-bootstrap.sh); deploy/nginx-vhost.conf is a reviewable sample of the same layout. The proxy must forward the browser's original Host header including the port (proxy_set_header Host $http_host;, never $host). See Security model for why.

gunicorn#

The shipped unit deploy/satom.service starts:

gunicorn --workers 4 --bind 127.0.0.1:8000 --timeout 600 \
  --access-logfile /var/log/satom/access.log \
  --error-logfile /var/log/satom/error.log wsgi:app

The unit binds to loopback, so only nginx can reach the application port, and a software update that re-copies the unit no longer re-opens 0.0.0.0:8000. The installer (installers/install-satom.sh) pins the service account through a systemd drop-in (see Services and timers).

ℹ️Note

Changed in 2.11.0: the shipped unit itself binds gunicorn to 127.0.0.1:8000 (before, only the installer's rewrite did, and an update could restore 0.0.0.0:8000); existing nodes get the corrected unit at their next update. The legacy deploy/install.sh bootstrap, which installed the unit as root, has been removed.

ℹ️Note — Worker model

The unit does not pass --threads or --worker-class, so gunicorn runs its default synchronous workers. The long --timeout 600 exists because Scout (AI assistant) replies are streamed and may legitimately hold a worker while the model is generating.

The application factory#

wsgi:app calls create_app() in app/__init__.py, which:

  • loads the configuration class selected by FLASK_ENV (production refuses to start without SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI);
  • initialises SQLAlchemy, Flask-Migrate, Flask-Login, CSRF protection (Flask-WTF), the rate limiter (Flask-Limiter) and Babel (UI language);
  • registers about 95 blueprints; FortiWeb-scoped blueprints are mounted under /web, and a missing blueprint module is skipped instead of stopping start-up;
  • installs the request gates, the security headers and the error handlers;
  • exposes unauthenticated health probes: /healthz, /healthz/primary, /healthz/backups and /healthz/cert-renewals;
  • seeds system profiles, the first admin account, reports, capacity limits, ADOMs, analytics boards, themes, ACME providers and the endpoint registry (the registry is reconciled to the shipped baseline, but rows an operator edited or disabled are never touched).

Request gates#

Gate Effect
Product (ADOM) gate Works out the effective product for the request (global, fortiweb, fortiadc, fortianalyzer, fortiauthenticator) and redirects away from pages that do not belong to it.
Access gate Applies the IP allow-list from Settings → Access Control. Users holding user_manage are exempt; an unreadable allow-list returns 503 instead of admitting everyone.
Device gate In the FortiWeb ADOM, per-device pages need a selected device; without one the user is sent to the Architecture view.
CSP nonce A nonce, stable for the session, is attached to every inline script and style.

The effective ADOM comes from a ?_adom= query parameter, else the X-ADOM header (sent by the browser tab on every Turbo visit and fetch), else an _adom form field on plain form posts, else the session default. Product pages then pin their own ADOM (for example the FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator pages, or a FortiWeb page opened from Global). Navigating never changes the session default; only an explicit switch does. See ADOMs and products.

Layers in the code#

app/views/*.py       HTTP handlers (Flask blueprints)
app/services/*.py    business logic, importable without a request context
app/clients/         REST clients per product + client_for(appliance)
app/registry/        endpoint registry loader (DB first, shipped JSON baseline fallback)
app/models*.py       SQLAlchemy models, one file per domain
app/api_v1/          the token-authenticated public REST API
app/api/             internal JSON endpoints used by the UI
app/templates, app/static   Jinja templates, Turbo Drive, vendored JS/CSS

Dependencies point one way: views → services → clients / registry / models. Services never assume a browser request, which is what lets the scheduler and background jobs run the same code headless.

Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework#

SATOM is mapped to the NAF Framework (Network Automation Forum, commit da82b12), the vendor-neutral reference model of six functional building blocks around the network infrastructure. Read against that model, the layers above sort into blocks: the Template Library, bindings and baselines are the Intent; the Source of Truth, the metrics store, the health engine and Sentinel are the Observability (the "Source of Truth" name predates the mapping — it holds the actual state, not the desired one); device sync, deep capture, the scrape targets, SNMP polling and the syslog receiver are the Collector; the CLI writer and the write actions are the Executor; Processes, Scheduled Actions and Change Requests are the Orchestrator; and the console, the satom command line and API v1 are the Presentation. Where SATOM sits in the NAF Framework explains each block in SATOM's words and the five names that collide; the conformance matrix with the current verdict is published with the product documentation (docs/naf-alignment.html, on a node at /manual/docs/naf-alignment.html).

Design principles#

Principle What it means in practice
Database-first reads Pages render from the local device cache in PostgreSQL; contacting an appliance is an explicit action (refresh, sync, save).
Preview before write Device changes are computed as a diff and shown before they are applied; applied changes are audited.
Registry-resolved URLs Code asks the endpoint registry for a logical endpoint name; the REST path for the product and API version comes from the registry, not from hard-coded strings.
Fail closed on partial knowledge For example, a configuration sync that returns zero objects is treated as an error and the existing cache is kept.
Per-appliance concurrency cap At most FORTINET_HOST_CONCURRENCY (default 4) concurrent requests per appliance, so workers, jobs and the scheduler together cannot flood a management plane.

Background work#

Jobs#

Long operations (firmware upload, upgrades, bulk pushes, discovery…) run as jobs: a daemon thread inside the gunicorn worker that started it, with its state kept as a JSON file in data/jobs/<id>.json. Any worker can read the state, so progress polling works no matter which worker answers. Stop and pause are cooperative: the request sets a flag in the job file and the job stops at its next safe checkpoint. See Jobs and Statuses.

POST requests on the device-facing pages are wrapped the same way: the request is replayed inside a job thread (with the same login, CSRF, ADOM and permission checks). If it finishes within SATOM_JOB_INLINE_S (default 2 s) the page gets the normal response; otherwise it gets a job reference and the job dock follows it. Writes to the same appliance queue behind each other ("Queued — waiting for …"). API-token calls and requests on a standby node are not wrapped.

Scheduler#

Scheduled Actions are fired by a separate process, never by the web workers (four workers would fire every action four times). satom-scheduler.service runs deploy/scheduler_guard.sh, which asks the local PostgreSQL whether it is a primary and only then starts app.scheduler_runtime; on a standby it waits and re-checks every 30 seconds. The scheduler ticks every 45 seconds, claims due actions with a database lease and runs each exactly once. An overdue action without catch-up is rolled forward and marked missed instead of being run late. See Scheduled actions.

Reconciler#

satom-reconciler.service runs on both nodes of a pair, ticking every 60 seconds. It does not start the Flask application; it reads the two settings it needs with psql and otherwise uses git and the update request queue. In MANUAL mode (the default) it only records drift; in AUTO mode it drives the staged self-update — standby first, then the primary, health-gated. See Software update.

Privileged runner#

The web application runs as an unprivileged account. Anything that needs root (installing units, upgrading libraries, restarting services, applying the PostgreSQL TLS protocol and cipher settings, promoting a standby) is written as a request file into data/update-requests/; the satom-updater.path unit notices it and starts the root-owned satom-updater.service, which re-validates the request against its own allow-list. See Security model.

Metrics store#

Fleet metrics are written to a local VictoriaMetrics instance (satom-metrics.service), bound to 127.0.0.1:8428 with a retention of 396 days. It has no authentication of its own, which is why it only listens on loopback and all queries go through the application. Configuration (boards, panels, targets, reports) stays in PostgreSQL. If the binary is missing, the rest of SATOM works and store-backed panels show a query error. See Metrics.

Two-node high availability#

Two nodes form a primary + standby pair. Failover is manual by design.

Concern How it is handled
Database PostgreSQL streaming replication; the standby is a read-only replica.
Files in data/ satom-ha-datasync.timer (cluster installs only) pulls data/ from the primary every 5 minutes with rsync over SSH, as the service account, restricted to a forced read-only command.
Scheduled actions Fire only where pg_is_in_recovery() is false (the primary).
Load balancer /healthz/primary returns 200 on the primary and 503 on a standby.
Code The reconciler keeps the standby on the primary's revision (AUTO mode).
Metrics store Per node; not replicated.
Failover An administrator confirms a promotion on the High Availability page; the privileged runner runs satom-promote.sh, which promotes PostgreSQL, starts the web app, restarts the scheduler and checks /healthz.

⚠️Warning — No automatic failover

With two PostgreSQL hosts and no quorum, an automatic promotion could create two primaries (split brain). Promotion is always an explicit operator action, taken when the old primary is known to be down. Re-attaching the old primary afterwards is a manual database job.

See High availability for the page and the procedure.

Advanced Where the role answer comes from

Every role-aware component asks the same question — SELECT pg_is_in_recovery() — using the application's own database credentials over TCP (deploy/satom-node-role.sh prints f for a primary or standalone node, t for a standby, and nothing if the database is not reachable). An earlier probe used runuser -u postgres, which needs root; once the units stopped running as root it returned nothing and every guard silently took the "not primary" branch.

Advanced Redis and the shared cache

Flask-Limiter reads RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI. With the default memory:// each gunicorn worker keeps its own counters; pointing it at redis:// makes all workers share one set of rate-limit buckets. The JSON cache in app/services/cache.py (key prefix fmcache:) uses CACHE_REDIS_URI, or the rate limiter's URI when that is a redis:// URL, and falls back to an in-process cache with a 30-second retry back-off when Redis is unavailable.

Advanced Health probes

/healthz returns ok, the running git revision (revision, sha, branch), a database summary, host statistics and peer_authenticated (whether the caller's request carried a valid node signature — an HMAC-SHA256 made with the shared node identity key, within 120 seconds of this node's clock). Without that signature it returns only ok and peer_authenticated. It is unauthenticated because the update runner and peer node use it. It does not prove that logins work: /healthz can answer 200 while the database password in .env is wrong.
